Roof Repair in Dallas

One weak spot is letting water in, or a storm loosened a few shingles. Call one free number day or night to reach an independent, locally owned roofing company that handles repairs in Dallas.

Call (469) 649-7066 Fix it or replace it?

What roof repair in Dallas usually means

Most roofs in Dallas that start leaking are not finished. They have one failure point: a rubber collar around a vent pipe that split after too many summers, a strip of metal at a wall that worked loose, or a handful of shingles that a spring gust peeled back. Fix that point properly and the roof can keep going for years.

This page is about those targeted fixes. It covers the problems roofers in Dallas find most often, how a careful roofer decides between patching and replacing, when the City of Dallas wants a permit, and what to ask before you agree to anything.

DFW Expert Roofers does not do repairs. It is a free phone number. Ring it at 3 a.m. or noon and a recorded assistant gathers two things, the roof trouble and your town, then patches you through to an independent roofer owned by local people. The inspection, price, repair and bill all belong to that roofer.

Six repairs Dallas roofers see again and again

North Texas weather works on a roof from several directions. The National Weather Service office in Fort Worth puts the normal at about 20 days a year of 100 degrees or more at DFW Airport, based on 1991 to 2020 records, and 2011 reached 71. Add spring hail and summer storm winds, and the same handful of weak spots keep showing up on service calls.

Split pipe boots

Plumbing vents pass through the roof inside a flexible collar. Sun and heat stiffen it until it cracks, and water runs down the pipe into a bathroom or hallway ceiling. On a sound roof this is one of the smallest repairs there is. The other boots are usually the same age, so ask about them too.

Loose wall and chimney flashing

Where a roof slope meets a brick wall, a chimney or a second story, thin metal pieces turn the water. When they slip, rust through or were only ever held with sealant, water gets behind them. Expect these drips to appear when rain blows sideways against that wall, then vanish in a calm shower. See roof flashing repair.

Lifted or missing shingles

Each shingle is nailed and also stuck to the course below by a sealant strip. A strong gust can break that bond. Some shingles blow off; others fall back flat and look fine while rain runs under them. A roofer checks the neighbors of every missing piece for broken seals. More on wind damage.

Hail bruises and cracks

Hail can knock granules loose and fracture the mat inside a shingle without leaving anything you would notice from the street. Months later the spot lets water through. Damage confined to one slope may be repairable; damage everywhere is a claim conversation. See hail damage roof repair.

Nails backing out

Decking swells and shrinks with heat and moisture, and over many seasons that movement can push a nail up until it lifts the shingle above it. The bump becomes a small hole. A repair pulls or resets the nail, seals the old hole and replaces the damaged shingle.

Worn valleys and ridge caps

Valleys carry the water from two slopes at once, and ridge caps sit in full sun from morning to evening. Both tend to wear out ahead of the field shingles. A worn valley can be rebuilt without touching the rest of the roof if the surrounding shingles are still flexible.

Leave the roof to the roofer. A wet or storm-hit roof is slippery, and damaged decking can give way, so keep off it and keep the ladder put away. Stay clear of any downed power line and report it to Oncor or your local electric utility, or call 911. Inside, pull furniture and electronics away from the drip, set out a bucket or towels, and keep everyone out of a room where the ceiling is sagging. Take photos from the yard and from inside, then call your insurance company and a roofer.

Repair or replace: a decision guide

A roofer standing on your roof makes this call, not a chart. These are the signs most roofers weigh, so you can follow the reasoning and ask for photos of whatever they point to.

What the roofer findsUsually points toWhy
One cracked boot, one loose flashing run, or a few missing shinglesRepairThe cause is local and the rest of the roof still sheds water.
Hail marks on a single slope of a roof under ten years oldRepair, possibly through a claimShingles may still be made in that color and line, so patches can blend.
Soft decking in one area under an old leakRepair with new deckingThe wet section is cut out and replaced, then shingled to match.
Bruising or cracking on most slopesReplacement, usually a claim questionPatching a roof that is damaged everywhere leaves the next leak waiting.
Brittle, curled shingles and granules piling up in guttersReplacementThe material itself is worn out, and new pieces will not seal to it.
Two layers of shingles already on the houseReplacement with full tear-offThe model residential code does not allow a third layer over two.

If replacement is recommended, ask what a repair would cost instead and how long the roofer expects it to hold. A straight answer to that question tells you a lot about the company. When a new roof is the answer, the roof replacement page explains tear-off, decking, permits and how to compare bids.

Permits for roof repair in the City of Dallas

The city's Development Services department publishes plain rules for storm and roof work. In short, small fixes go ahead without paperwork, while big ones need a permit pulled by a contractor the city has registered.

  • No permit: minor repairs to roofing or roof vents, and temporary tarps.
  • Re-roof permit: replacing large areas of a roof or the entire roof.
  • Building permit: replacing structural members such as rafters, roof joists or wall sections.
  • Who applies: a contractor, the owner or an agent may apply, but a registered contractor must be on the application before the permit is issued.
  • Owners doing their own work file a Homeowner's Exemption from Contractor Registration form instead of registering.

Questions go to the city at 214-948-4480. Plano, Fort Worth, Garland and the other cities in the metro write their own rules, and each town page notes what its city requires.

What a careful repair visit looks like

Your part is a phone call. The line asks a few questions and passes you to a roofing company; from there, a well-run repair tends to follow the same order.

  1. The roofer listens first. Where the stain is, when it drips, which way the wind was blowing, how old the roof is. Those answers narrow the search before anyone sets up a ladder.
  2. Roof and attic both get checked. Water travels along the deck and rafters before it drops, so the entry point is often uphill from the stain. A good roofer looks from below as well as above.
  3. You see what was found. Ask for photos of the failed boot, the gap in the flashing or the broken seal, taken that day.
  4. The estimate is written and itemized. Shingles by brand and line, flashing, boots, and decking priced per sheet if any turns up rotten. It should say whether a part is replaced or just sealed.
  5. The cause is fixed, not covered. New metal or a new boot where one failed. A smear of roof cement over a gap is a stopgap and should be priced and labeled as one.
  6. The area is cleaned up and nails swept from the beds and driveway, with the workmanship warranty, if any, written on the invoice.

Questions to ask before you say yes to a repair

About the work

  • What exactly failed, and can you show me a photo?
  • Will you replace the part or seal it, and how long should each option last?
  • Are matching shingles still made for my roof, and what happens if they are not?
  • Did you see the same problem anywhere else on the roof?

About who is doing it

  • Will your insurer email me a current liability certificate directly?
  • Are you registered with my city, if my city registers roofers?
  • What workmanship warranty comes with a repair, and is it in writing?
  • When do you expect payment, and is any deposit required for a small job?

Many roofers will look at a roof at no charge, though policies differ, so ask about that during the call.

Small habits that keep repairs small

The National Roofing Contractors Association recommends a roof check at least twice a year, spring and fall, plus another after any severe storm, and after a storm it tells owners to look only from the ground. In practice that means walking around the house with your phone camera, looking for shingles in the yard, dark patches, sagging gutters or metal bent at the edges.

Indoors, glance at ceilings in upstairs rooms and closets after heavy rain. If the attic has a safe floored area by the hatch, a look with a flashlight from that spot can show a damp patch early. Leave anything beyond that to the roofer. Catching a split boot in April usually means a short repair; finding it after a summer of storms can mean new decking and drywall as well.

Seen a stain, a missing shingle or bent metal and not sure how serious it is? Describe it on the phone and you are transferred to a Dallas-area roofing company that does repairs.

How a repair call goes

  1. Dial the lineAn automated assistant picks up (469) 649-7066 any time and asks what you need. The same number also takes air conditioning, heating and pressure washing calls, so say "roof".
  2. Tell it about the roofHail, a drip in the ceiling, shingles in the yard, a tree limb, or an aging roof you want checked, plus your town and how soon you need someone.
  3. Get transferredThe call goes to an independent roofing company that is locally owned and works in Dallas-Fort Worth. It hears a quick summary of your call before it answers.
  4. Work with that companyIt inspects, prices and does the job, and you pay it (or your insurer does, as you arrange). If it cannot pick up, it gets your name, number, town and need so it can call you back.

No state license for roofers. Texas does not license roofing contractors. A 2025 bill that would have had the state license re-roofers (HB 3344) cleared a House committee but never got a floor vote, and it died when the session ended. That puts the checking on you: ask for a certificate of liability insurance sent to you by the roofer's insurance agent or insurer, a written contract that lists the full scope, the permit or contractor registration your city requires, addresses of nearby jobs, and proof the shingle warranty was registered. The line does none of this checking for you. How to check a roofer in Texas.

Your deductible is yours to pay. The Texas Department of Insurance warns that a contractor may not waive your deductible, rebate it, or pad the estimate to cover it, and that a contract of $1,000 or more paid with insurance money must include a notice that you owe the deductible. Your insurer may ask for proof you paid it. A contractor also may not act as a public adjuster on a property it works on or may work on. If a roofer offers to "take care of" the deductible, hire someone else.

Dallas roof repair questions

Do I need a city permit to repair my roof in Dallas?

Usually not for a small job. The City of Dallas says minor repairs to roofing or roof vents need no permit, and neither does a temporary tarp. Replacing a large area or the whole roof calls for a re-roof permit, and replacing rafters or joists calls for a building permit. A contractor registered with the city has to be on the application. Suburbs set their own rules, so check your town page.

How often should a roof get maintenance in North Texas?

The National Roofing Contractors Association suggests a roof be looked at at least twice a year, in spring and fall, and again after any hail, tornado or severe wind. For a homeowner that means a look from the yard and the attic hatch, never from a ladder. A roofer can do the close-up check. The roof inspection page lists what a thorough one covers.

What does roof repair cost in Dallas?

The line does not set or quote prices, and no fair number exists before someone sees the roof. Cost follows what failed (a boot, a run of flashing, a section of decking), the pitch and height, how many layers are on the house, and whether the matching shingle is still made. Get the estimate on paper with every part and labor charge broken out. For full roofs, the DFW replacement cost guide explains what drives the number.

Can hail damage be repaired, or does it mean a whole new roof?

It depends on how far the damage spreads. A few cracked shingles on one slope can often be replaced individually if the shingle is still sold. Bruising across several slopes usually points to replacement, and an adjuster decides what a claim covers. Ask the roofer for dated photos of each damaged area. The hail damage page covers what to look for.

If I call about a roof repair, whose crew shows up?

A crew from an independent, owner-run roofing company that takes repair work in your corner of DFW. DFW Expert Roofers never sends anyone; it is a switchboard. The automated assistant hears your description and puts the call through, and from that point the roofing company handles the visit, the price, the repair and the bill. Calling costs you nothing. Roofing companies on the line may pay it a fee for referrals, which is why it is free to you.
